name: Internal impingement in the overhead athlete
aka: articular-sided cuff and labral lesions in throwers
summary: Pain at the back of the shoulder in late cocking as the cuff undersurface meets the posterosuperior glenoid. Some contact is physiological, the GIRD link is debated and treatment evidence is limited.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: Weeks to months of load management, rotation-range work and scapular, cuff and kinetic-chain training; no controlled treatment trials in symptomatic throwers were found

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: After arthroscopic surgery in 135 throwers, 90% returned to sport but only 52% to the previous sport at the same level (mean follow-up 7.9 years)

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Posterior shoulder pain reproduced in the throwing position (90° abduction, full external rotation); no validated accuracy figures. Measure internal and total rotation range

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: MRI findings are common in pain-free throwers: the labrum was abnormal in 79% of 28 shoulders of 14 asymptomatic pitchers

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Young adult throwers: mean age 25 years in the original arthroscopic series of 17 athletes

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Not established; described by surgeons as the leading cause of chronic shoulder pain in overhead throwers

overview:
Internal impingement is contact between the deep surface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus and the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum when the arm is abducted to about 90° and maximally externally rotated, the late-cocking position of throwing. Walch and colleagues described it arthroscopically in 17 athletes with unexplained pain on throwing, finding impingement of the undersurface of the cuff on the posterosuperior glenoid, partial cuff tears in all, and posterosuperior labral lesions in 12 [r1]. It is better thought of as a constellation of problems, including articular-sided cuff tears, labral tears, biceps tendinitis, anterior instability, internal rotation deficit and scapular dysfunction [r2].

Be honest about what is pathological. Loaded arm movements produce a physiological contact between the posterosuperior edge of the glenoid and the deep aspect of the cuff [r3]. Shoulder MRI findings are common in throwers without symptoms: the labrum was abnormal in 79% of 28 shoulders of 14 asymptomatic professional pitchers [r4]; 8 of 20 dominant shoulders (40%) of elite overhead athletes had cuff tears and none had symptoms 5 years later [r5]; and 11 of 21 asymptomatic professional pitchers had a cuff tear and 10 a SLAP tear, correlated with innings pitched but not with later time on the disabled list [r6]. The glenohumeral internal rotation deficit (GIRD) is also common in pain-free pitchers and is related to humeral retroversion [r7], and recent reviews conclude that GIRD alone is not clearly linked with injury risk [r8,r9].

The evidence is mostly observational. Treatment is non-operative first, with a focus on restoring range of motion and scapular function [r2], but controlled trials in symptomatic throwers are lacking: the best evidence is for stretching in pain-free or non-athletic groups [r10,r11]. Surgical results are variable: in 135 throwers treated arthroscopically 90% returned to sport but 52% to the previous sport at the same level [r12], and an earlier series of 75 athletes had 60% disappointed after debridement [r3].

epidemiology.text: Reliable incidence figures for internal impingement were not found. Authors describe it as the leading cause of chronic shoulder pain in overhead throwing athletes [r12]. The original arthroscopic series had 17 athletes with a mean age of 25 years (range 15–30) and symptoms for a mean of 27 months [r1]. A series of 75 throwers had pain for a mean of 22.3 months, and 89% had partial tears of the deep cuff, which were associated with a labral lesion in 90% [r3]. Imaging findings are highly prevalent in pain-free throwers [r4,r5,r6] and GIRD of more than 25° was found in 10 of 23 asymptomatic professional pitchers [r7], so prevalence of 'findings' far exceeds prevalence of symptomatic disease.

intrinsic: Physiological adaptations to throwing: increased external rotation, increased humeral and glenoid retroversion and anterior laxity may predispose to internal impingement [r2]
Posterior capsule and soft tissue tightness with GIRD: posterior capsule hypertrophy was moderately related to soft-tissue GIRD in 45 healthy pitchers (r = 0.40) [r13]
Scapular dyskinesis, particularly scapular protraction with glenoid antetilt and posterior humeral head translation [r14]
A total rotation deficit of more than 5° compared with the other shoulder, associated with a higher rate of injury in professional pitchers [r15]
Capsular contracture after repetitive external rotation, which shifts the humeral head posterosuperiorly [r16]
extrinsic: Repetitive overhead throwing: career innings pitched correlated with cuff and labral findings in asymptomatic pitchers [r6]
Throwing and overhead sports with maximal abduction and external rotation (baseball, softball, tennis, volleyball, handball) [r2]
High throwing workload without adequate recovery, particularly after a sudden increase (clinical convention)

mechanism.summary: In late cocking the arm is abducted to about 90° and maximally externally rotated. The greater tuberosity and the undersurface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus then contact the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum, a contact that is physiological in many throwers [r3,r1]. Capsular contracture after repetitive external rotation shifts the humeral head posterosuperiorly, and scapular protraction with glenoid antetilt adds posterior translation of the head; together these predispose to symptomatic internal impingement [r16,r14]. Repetition can then produce articular-sided partial cuff tears, posterosuperior labral lesions and humeral head cysts [r1,r16].
sequence: The thrower brings the arm into late cocking, abducted to about 90° and maximally externally rotated [r1].
The humeral head rotates backward and the undersurface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus contacts the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum, normally a physiological contact [r3].

Repeated throws, in a shoulder with increased external rotation, humeral retroversion, a tight posterior capsule or scapular dyskinesis, drive the head posterosuperiorly with more force or at more extreme positions [r2,r14,r16].
The cuff undersurface and the posterosuperior labrum are injured, with articular-sided partial tears and labral fraying; humeral head cysts and 'kissing' lesions can appear on imaging [r16,r1].
Pain appears in late cocking and early acceleration, with reduced velocity and control.
The thrower compensates (altered scapular and trunk motion), which may increase load on the shoulder further (a proposed cycle, not directly measured).

variants.name: Classic throwing (baseball and softball)
variants.description: The original description: pain in the late-cocking position, with undersurface cuff and posterosuperior labral lesions in athletes without anterior instability [r1].

variants.name: Other overhead sports
variants.description: Racquet sports, volleyball, handball and swimming involve similar repeated abduction and external rotation, and the same pattern is described in overhead athletes generally [r2].

variants.name: Internal impingement with subtle instability
variants.description: Some athletes have anterior laxity or microinstability that adds to the contact, and addressing microinstability is considered important when surgery is chosen [r2]. Walch noted that internal impingement sits beside Neer's impingement syndrome and Jobe's instability with secondary impingement [r1].

variants.name: Asymptomatic adaptation
variants.description: Many throwers have posterosuperior contact, GIRD and cuff or labral changes without symptoms or later problems [r4,r5,r7]. Symptoms and function, not the finding, define the problem.

anatomy.text: In the throwing position the posterior cuff undersurface (supraspinatus and infraspinatus insertions) lies against the posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum. The posterior capsule and the posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament limit internal rotation and tighten with repeated throwing, and the humeral shaft in throwers is more retroverted, which increases external rotation range at the cost of internal rotation [r2,r8]. The scapula and clavicle move together with the humerus (scapulohumeral rhythm) to place the glenoid under the head, and altered scapular motion can change how the head contacts the glenoid [r14].

structures.name: Posterosuperior glenoid rim and labrum
structures.role: The site of contact in late cocking; labral lesions occur here [r1,r3]

structures.name: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus (articular surface)
structures.role: The undersurface contacts the glenoid rim; articular-sided partial tears are the typical lesion [r1,r3]

structures.name: Posterior capsule and posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
structures.role: Tighten or thicken with repeated throwing, contributing to soft-tissue GIRD [r13,r16]

structures.name: Humeral head and greater tuberosity
structures.role: May develop cysts from repeated contact; humeral retroversion adapts in throwers [r16,r8]

structures.name: Long head of biceps and superior labrum
structures.role: The biceps-labral anchor can peel back in the same position (see SLAP lesion) [r16]

structures.name: Scapular stabilisers
structures.role: Control glenoid position; scapular protraction and antetilt promote posterior humeral head translation [r14]

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
In Walch's arthroscopic series of 17 throwers, the humerus placed in the throwing position showed impingement between the posterosuperior glenoid and the undersurface of the supraspinatus and infraspinatus; partial cuff ruptures were confirmed in 8 by arthrogram and a further 9 had a partial capsulotendinous rupture that the arthrogram missed, and 12 had lesions of the posterosuperior labrum [r1]. In 75 throwers, 89% had partial deep-surface cuff tears and 90% of these also had a labral lesion, usually fissures behind the biceps insertion, with damage to glenoid and humeral head cartilage [r3]. Imaging can show humeral head cysts and 'kissing' tears of the posterosuperior cuff and labrum [r16].

The contributions of bone and soft tissue to GIRD differ. GIRD has an adaptive bony component (humeral retroversion), and muscular and capsular components that confound it [r8]; posterior capsule hypertrophy is moderately related to soft-tissue GIRD (r = 0.40) [r13]. Because GIRD, posterosuperior contact and structural change all occur in people without symptoms [r7,r4,r5,r6], the pathological element is the combination of overload, symptoms and loss of function rather than any single finding.

structures.name: Undersurface of supraspinatus and infraspinatus
structures.effect: Articular-sided partial tears: 89% of 75 throwers had partial tears of the deep cuff [r3]

structures.name: Posterosuperior labrum
structures.effect: The labrum was fissured in 52% and fringed in 38% of 75 throwers, mostly behind the biceps insertion [r3]; lesions were present in 12 of 17 in the original series [r1]

structures.name: Posterior capsule
structures.effect: Capsular contracture and thickening shift the head posterosuperiorly and contribute to soft-tissue GIRD [r16,r13]

structures.name: Humeral head and glenoid cartilage
structures.effect: Cysts and cartilage wear from repeated contact [r16,r3]

structures.name: Humeral retroversion
structures.effect: Bony adaptation that increases external rotation and reduces internal rotation without being soft-tissue tightness [r8,r7]

muscles.name: Infraspinatus and teres minor
muscles.effect: Posterior cuff muscles that take eccentric load in deceleration; tightness is associated with soft-tissue GIRD, and their endurance matters (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Scapular stabilisers (serratus anterior, lower trapezius)
muscles.effect: Dyskinesis with protraction and antetilt contributes to posterior head translation and internal impingement [r14]

muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi, teres major and pectoralis minor
muscles.effect: Tightness can restrict scapular positioning and rotation range (clinical reasoning)

muscles.name: Trunk and hip muscles
muscles.effect: Proximal factors affect arm load; evaluation of throwers should include proximal and distal causative factors [r14]

cellular.description: Repeated overload of the cuff undersurface produces a reactive tendon response with cell activation and matrix swelling; in many throwers this is subclinical.
With continued overload, matrix disorganisation and increased ground substance occur, and symptoms may appear.
Areas of cell loss and disorganised matrix (articular-sided partial tear) can develop; many such changes are present without symptoms [r6,r5].

systems.effect: Pain, altered scapular and cuff motor control and a loss of confidence in the late-cocking position; central processing may sustain symptoms even after the tissues settle.
Hip, trunk and scapular control change the load at late cocking; scapular dyskinesis is common in throwers with internal impingement [r14].
Increased humeral retroversion in throwers is a bony adaptation to throwing and is not soft-tissue tightness [r8,r7].
Pressure to continue throwing, fear of surgery or losing a place in a team, and expectations from imaging findings affect decisions.
Synovitis and capsular irritation accompany symptomatic episodes and settle with load management.

timeframes.summary: No controlled study reports a recovery timeline for symptomatic internal impingement. In practice, rotation range and scapular and cuff control take weeks, strengthening and kinetic-chain work take months, and return to full throwing follows an interval throwing program (clinical convention). After arthroscopic surgery in 135 throwers, outcomes were assessed at a mean of 7.9 years [r12].

healing.description: Relative rest from throwing and provocative positions, keep moving, and begin scapular and cuff activation.

healing.phase: Restore rotation range and scapular control
healing.description: Posterior shoulder mobility work if tight, scapular and cuff endurance, and thoracic mobility.
Progressive cuff, scapular, trunk and lower-limb strength and power with graded exposure to abduction and external rotation.
Plyometrics and a graded interval throwing program, criteria-based.

milestones.label: Total rotation arc symmetrical and scapular control restored
Return to competitive throwing
milestones.note: Criteria-based, commonly about 3–6 months after non-operative care (clinical convention); later after surgery

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based. No controlled data on non-operative return were found. After arthroscopic surgery in 135 throwers, 90% returned to sport but only 52% to the previous sport at the same level [r12]. Time alone is not a criterion.

symptoms: Posterior or posterosuperior shoulder pain in the late-cocking and early acceleration phases of throwing [r1]
Reduced velocity, control or endurance, and pain after throwing
Stiffness at the back of the shoulder and difficulty reaching across the body
Insidious onset over weeks to months, with symptoms often present for a year or more before surgical referral [r1,r3]
Pain usually settles with rest but returns on resuming throwing
signs: Localised pain on full external rotation at 90° abduction, and sometimes a positive impingement sign [r1]
GIRD and a reduced total rotation arc compared with the other shoulder
Posterior joint line and posterior cuff tenderness
Signs of a partial cuff tear (pain and weakness on resisted external rotation) in some [r1]

subjective: Phase of throwing that hurts (late cocking, acceleration, deceleration), and whether the pain is posterior, anterior or deep
Throwing volume, recent changes in workload, number of seasons and level of competition, and any changes in velocity or control
Previous injury and treatment, including elbow problems, and symptoms elsewhere in the kinetic chain
Age and skeletal maturity: pain in an adolescent thrower raises the possibility of a physeal problem (see Little League shoulder)
Instability symptoms (slipping, 'dead arm') and neurological or vascular symptoms
Goals, season timing and willingness to modify throwing load
observation: Scapular position at rest and dyskinesis during elevation and lowering, particularly protraction [r14]
Posture: thoracic kyphosis, forward head and shoulder protraction
Muscle bulk of infraspinatus and supraspinatus, and any wasting
Throwing mechanics and the kinetic chain from video if available
palpation: Posterior joint line and posterior cuff tenderness
AC joint, trapezius and scapular muscle tone
rangeOfMotion: Passive internal and external rotation at 90° abduction with the scapula stabilised, side to side; total rotation arc (external plus internal rotation) [r15]
Interpret GIRD with the total arc and, where available, humeral retroversion: a deficit in internal rotation may be matched by a gain in external rotation [r8,r7]
Horizontal adduction (cross-body) and shoulder flexion, side to side
Thoracic rotation and extension, and hip rotation
strength: External and internal rotation strength (hand-held dynamometry), comparing sides, and posterior cuff endurance
Scapular strength and endurance (serratus anterior, lower and middle trapezius)
Resisted abduction and external rotation for cuff pain or weakness
neuro: Cervical screen to exclude cervical radiculopathy
Suprascapular nerve: infraspinatus bulk and external rotation strength if wasting or paralabral cyst is suspected
Vascular symptoms with throwing (arm fatigue, cold or discoloured hand) should prompt specialist review
functional: Throwing in a graded program: symptom response at each stage
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test and single-arm seated shot-put
Single-leg balance and squat, trunk rotation and hip rotation (kinetic-chain screen)

specialTests.name: Throwing-position provocation (full external rotation at 90° abduction)
specialTests.purpose: Reproduce posterior pain from posterosuperior internal impingement
specialTests.procedure: Supine or standing, abduct the arm to about 90° and externally rotate to the end of range, adding slight extension, and ask where the pain is.
specialTests.positive: Posterior or posterosuperior pain in the throwing position. Walch described localised pain on full external rotation at 90° abduction in his series [r1]. No sensitivity or specificity figures for this test were found in the sources reviewed, so none are quoted.

specialTests.name: Relocation test (Jobe)
specialTests.purpose: Differentiate internal impingement with anterior microinstability from a purely structural problem
specialTests.procedure: Supine, arm abducted to 90° and externally rotated until pain or apprehension; apply a posteriorly directed force on the proximal humerus and note any relief.
specialTests.positive: Relief of pain with the posterior force is taken to suggest anterior laxity or microinstability contributing to the impingement (clinical reasoning); anterior instability and microinstability are part of the constellation described for internal impingement [r2]. No accuracy figures for internal impingement were found in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: Glenohumeral rotation range and total arc
specialTests.purpose: Identify GIRD and a total rotation deficit
specialTests.procedure: Supine, shoulder abducted to 90° in the scapular plane with the scapula stabilised anteriorly, measure passive external and internal rotation with a goniometer or inclinometer, and compare with the other shoulder. Add external plus internal rotation to give the total arc.
specialTests.positive: GIRD is commonly defined as a loss of internal rotation of 20° or more compared with the other shoulder [r15], although 18° to 20° may be too conservative for adults and different for adolescents [r17]. In 819 overhead athletes the weighted mean GIRD was 13.8° in injured versus 9.6° in uninjured athletes [r17]. A total rotation deficit of more than 5° was associated with a higher injury rate in professional pitchers [r15]. GIRD is common in pain-free pitchers (over 25° in 10 of 23) [r7], so it is a measurement, not a diagnosis.

specialTests.name: Scapular dyskinesis assessment
specialTests.purpose: Identify scapular contribution to posterior humeral head translation
specialTests.procedure: Observe the scapula during loaded elevation and lowering and during a throwing-like movement; assist or reposition the scapula and note the effect on pain.
specialTests.positive: Scapular protraction, glenoid antetilt or winging, and symptom relief when the scapula is assisted, suggest that scapular dysfunction contributes [r14]. No accuracy figures from the sources reviewed are quoted.

clinicalRules.name: GIRD is a measurement, not a diagnosis
clinicalRules.description: Recent literature shows that GIRD alone is not associated with upper limb injury risk in overhead athletes; other deficits (external rotation, horizontal adduction, flexion) are associated with injury, and adaptive (bony) GIRD should be separated from pathological soft-tissue GIRD [r8]. A systematic review found a standardised mean difference in GIRD of 0.46 between injured and uninjured overhead athletes [r17], while a meta-analysis found a mean difference of 3.11° that did not reach significance (95% CI −0.13° to 6.36°) [r9].

clinicalRules.name: Do not treat the scan
clinicalRules.description: Cuff tears, labral lesions, SLAP tears and Bennett lesions are common on MRI in pain-free throwers, and MRI alone should not be a basis for operative intervention [r5,r4,r6]. Correlate with the symptoms, the throwing position and the examination.

outcomeMeasures.name: Kerlan-Jobe Orthopaedic Clinic (KJOC) shoulder and elbow score
outcomeMeasures.use: Overhead-athlete function; used with Constant's score in the 135-patient surgical series [r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: Constant score
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective shoulder function; used in surgical follow-up [r12]

outcomeMeasures.name: Passive glenohumeral rotation range and total arc
Hand-held dynamometry and the Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
outcomeMeasures.use: Strength limb symmetry and functional readiness before return to throwing

outcomeMeasures.name: Pain with throwing and number of throws completed in an interval program

imaging.indication: Persistent pain, to look for Bennett lesions, glenohumeral osteoarthritis or other bone pathology
imaging.findings: Posteroinferior glenoid exostosis (Bennett lesion) and bony changes; these are common in asymptomatic throwers [r5]

imaging.indication: Persistent pain after a trial of rehabilitation, suspected full-thickness cuff or large labral tear, or surgical planning
imaging.findings: Partial articular-sided cuff tears, posterosuperior labral lesions, SLAP tears and humeral head cysts, with 'kissing' lesions [r16]. These are frequent in pain-free throwers: the labrum was abnormal in 79% of asymptomatic pitchers' shoulders [r4], 40% of dominant shoulders had cuff tears [r5], and 11 of 21 pitchers had cuff tears [r6].

imaging.indication: Cuff tear screening and measurement of posterior capsule thickness or humeral retroversion where available
imaging.findings: Posterior capsule hypertrophy was related to soft-tissue GIRD in pitchers [r13]; ultrasound is reliable and valid for measuring humeral retroversion [r8].

differentials.name: SLAP lesion
differentials.distinguishing: Deep pain with mechanical symptoms and biceps-labrum provocation; often coexists with internal impingement.

differentials.name: Rotator cuff related shoulder pain (subacromial)
differentials.distinguishing: Painful arc and pain with resisted abduction or elevation, rather than posterior pain in late cocking.

differentials.name: Anterior shoulder instability
differentials.distinguishing: Dislocation or subluxation history, apprehension and a positive relocation test with anterior pain.

differentials.name: Multidirectional instability
differentials.distinguishing: Generalised laxity, a positive sulcus sign and symptoms in several directions.

differentials.name: Posterior shoulder instability
differentials.distinguishing: A clunk with the arm flexed, adducted and internally rotated (jerk and Kim tests) rather than pain in late cocking.

differentials.name: Little League shoulder (proximal humeral epiphysiolysis)
differentials.distinguishing: An adolescent with open growth plates, lateral or proximal humeral pain on throwing and physeal widening on radiograph.

differentials.name: Long head of biceps tendinopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Anterior pain over the bicipital groove with resisted flexion and supination.

differentials.name: Thoracic outlet syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Neurovascular symptoms (arm heaviness, paraesthesia, colour change) with overhead throwing rather than posterior pain.

differentials.name: Cervical radiculopathy
differentials.distinguishing: Neck-origin pain with dermatomal symptoms, reproduced by Spurling or neck movements.

redFlags: Sudden pop with immediate loss of throwing ability, weakness or inability to elevate the arm: possible full-thickness cuff tear or proximal biceps or pectoralis major rupture. Arrange imaging and orthopaedic review.
Arm fatigue, coldness, pallor, discolouration or numbness with throwing (vascular thoracic outlet or axillary artery problems in throwers): specialist vascular review.

Neurological deficit (weakness, wasting, reflex change), particularly isolated infraspinatus wasting: cervical, brachial plexus or suprascapular nerve problem (for example a paralabral cyst). Refer for imaging and nerve assessment.
An adolescent thrower with persistent proximal humeral pain: consider Little League shoulder (physeal injury); obtain radiographs and rest from throwing.
Constant night or rest pain, fever, weight loss or a history of cancer: consider infection or tumour and refer urgently for imaging.
Chest pressure, breathlessness or sweating with shoulder pain: seek urgent medical assessment for cardiac or visceral causes.
After surgery: fever, wound drainage, erythema or severe escalating pain suggest infection; refer back to the surgeon the same day.

management.principles: Treat the whole thrower, not the scan. Non-operative management is attempted first and focuses on restoring range of motion and improving scapular function [r2], then cuff, trunk and lower-limb capacity and a graded return to throwing. Be honest with the athlete: some posterosuperior contact, GIRD and cuff and labral findings are normal adaptations to throwing [r3,r7,r4], GIRD alone is not clearly linked with injury risk [r8,r9], and the evidence for any treatment in symptomatic throwers is limited. The best evidence is for stretching in pain-free or non-athletic groups [r10,r11]. Surgery is for the minority who fail an adequate program; results are variable and many throwers do not return to the same level [r12,r3], and addressing microinstability matters when operating [r2].

medical.name: Relative rest, load modification and analgesia
medical.description: Short-term analgesia and a temporary reduction in throwing volume and intensity to settle the irritable shoulder, with a plan to return gradually. No trial evidence was found for the amount or duration of rest.

medical.name: Arthroscopic debridement of the posterosuperior labrum and partial cuff tear (after failed rehabilitation)
medical.description: In 75 throwers with a mean of 22.3 months of pain who failed conservative treatment, only 8 were very satisfied and 22 satisfied after arthroscopic debridement, 45 were disappointed (60%), only 12 resumed their former level with loaded arm movements, and 22 had another procedure (20 humeral derotation osteotomies) [r3]. In 135 throwers treated with several arthroscopic procedures, 90% returned to sport and 52% to the previous sport at the same level at a mean of 7.9 years; cuff tear debridement was associated with a better return-to-sport outcome in univariate analysis [r12]. Both are uncontrolled series.

medical.name: Anterior capsulorrhaphy for suspected microinstability
medical.description: Addressing microinstability is considered important when surgery is chosen [r2], but in the 135-patient series anterior capsulorrhaphy was associated with worse postoperative pain [r12]. A specialist decision after careful examination under anaesthesia.

medical.name: Surgery based on an MRI finding alone
medical.description: Cuff tears, labral lesions and other findings are common in pain-free throwers (for example 79% abnormal labra in asymptomatic pitchers [r4]; 40% of dominant shoulders with cuff tears and none symptomatic at 5 years [r5]), and MRI alone should not be used as the basis for surgery [r5].

physio.name: Graded throwing load management and interval throwing program
physio.description: Reduce, then progressively reload throwing volume and intensity using an interval program, with symptom response guiding progression; consider workload spikes and mechanics. No controlled trial of a throwing program in symptomatic internal impingement was found.

physio.name: Scapular, rotator cuff and kinetic-chain training
physio.description: Non-operative treatment focuses on increasing range of motion and improving scapular function [r2]. Scapular dyskinesis with protraction contributes to posterior head translation and internal impingement, and evaluation should follow a pathway through proximal and distal causes [r14]. This reflects expert review rather than trial evidence.

physio.name: Posterior shoulder stretching (cross-body, modified sleeper) for posterior tightness or GIRD
physio.description: A systematic review of 10 randomised trials found moderate evidence of positive immediate and short-term effects of the cross-body stretch on posterior shoulder tightness and GIRD in asymptomatic young people, and moderate evidence that the active sleeper stretch might not be more effective than no intervention in the short term; long-term effects in symptomatic patients are unknown [r10]. In 34 male volleyball players with posterior shoulder tightness, a 6-week program of sleeper and cross-body stretches improved internal rotation, spike velocity and seated shot-put distance, but tissue stiffness did not change [r11]. In a cross-sectional study of 85 professional pitchers, those in an internal rotation stretching program for 3 or more years had greater internal rotation (74.3° versus 54.3°) and total range (217.0° versus 194.2°) than those with less than 3 years, which cannot show cause and effect [r18]. Stretching addresses the soft-tissue part of GIRD, not bony retroversion [r8].

physio.name: Education about adaptation and imaging findings
physio.description: Explain that posterosuperior contact, GIRD and cuff or labral findings are common in pain-free throwers [r3,r4,r5], that symptoms and function guide treatment, and that the aim is to restore load tolerance. Agree on workload, a return plan and when to revisit imaging or surgery.

physio.name: Treating GIRD in isolation, or stretching to 'normalise' range in pain-free throwers
physio.description: GIRD alone is not clearly associated with injury risk; part of it is adaptive bone rather than soft tissue [r8,r9,r7], and in a 2018 meta-analysis the difference between injured and uninjured athletes was small (a mean GIRD of 13.8° versus 9.6°) [r17]. Treat the thrower with symptoms and a measurable soft-tissue deficit, not the number alone.

education: Some contact between the back of the shoulder socket and the rotator cuff is normal when throwing, and many throwers have scan findings and reduced inward rotation without pain.
Treatment aims to restore your throwing capacity: shoulder-blade control, rotator cuff strength, back-of-shoulder mobility if tight, and strength and timing through the legs and trunk.
The evidence for individual treatments is limited, so we will track your pain, range and throwing tolerance and adjust the plan.
Surgery is for the few who do not improve with a full program; results vary and many throwers do not return to exactly the same level [r12,r3].
Tell your clinician about a sudden pop and loss of power, a cold or discoloured arm with throwing, or night pain that does not ease.

rehab.overview: Progression is criteria-based and rotates between regaining rotation range and scapular control, building strength and kinetic-chain capacity, and graded throwing. No controlled trial of a full program in symptomatic internal impingement was found, so the program below reflects expert guidance (restore range and scapular function first [r2]) and the limited stretching evidence [r10,r11]. Dosages are typical clinical conventions and criteria override time.

stages.name: Settle and modify load
goals: Keep the shoulder moving in comfortable range
Begin scapular and posterior cuff activation
Educate on load and the plan
precautions: Rest from throwing and provocative end-range cocking
Avoid forcing end-range external rotation at 90° abduction
Seek review if there is a sudden pop, weakness or vascular symptoms

exercises.name: Pendulum (Codman) swings
exercises.cues: Let the arm hang loose and swing by moving the trunk

exercises.name: Scapular setting (retraction and depression)
exercises.cues: Draw the shoulder blades back and down without shrugging

exercises.name: Submaximal isometric external rotation at the side
exercises.dosage: 5 × 10 s at 20–30% effort, twice daily (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Elbow bent, arm at the side, press gently into the wall

exercises.name: Cross-body adduction stretch (gentle)
exercises.cues: Pull the arm across the chest to a mild stretch at the back of the shoulder, not pain

progressionCriteria: Resting pain 3/10 or less and sleeping without regular waking
Pain-free daily activities and elevation to about 120°
Able to hold the scapula set during arm movement

stages.name: Restore rotation range and scapular control
goals: Restore a symmetrical total rotation arc if soft-tissue tightness is present
Improve scapular control and cuff endurance
precautions: Stretch to mild tension only; the sleeper stretch can provoke posterosuperior pain
Do not stretch away a bony adaptation: measure total arc, not internal rotation alone [r8]

exercises.name: Modified sleeper stretch or cross-body stretch
exercises.cues: Gentle internal rotation or horizontal adduction; stop at first firm stretch

exercises.name: Side-lying external rotation
exercises.dosage: 2–3 × 15 with a light dumbbell, 3–4 times per week
exercises.cues: Elbow tucked to the ribs, rotate slowly

exercises.name: Band row and wall slide
exercises.cues: Squeeze the shoulder blades back and down; keep them moving on the wall

exercises.name: Thoracic extension over a foam roller
exercises.cues: Support the head, extend over the roller and breathe out

exercises.name: Quadruped bird-dog
exercises.cues: Keep the shoulder blades set and the trunk still

progressionCriteria: Total rotation arc symmetrical or within about 5° of the other side (clinical convention)
Normal scapular rhythm on elevation and lowering
No pain with daily activities and gentle overhead tasks

stages.name: Strength and kinetic chain
goals: Restore strength to near the other side
Rebuild tolerance for abduction and external rotation
precautions: Introduce 90° abduction and external rotation loading gradually
Do not start plyometrics until strength and control criteria are met

exercises.name: External rotation at 90° abduction with a band
exercises.dosage: 3 × 10–12, increase range gradually, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Stable shoulder blade; stop before the range provokes posterior pain

exercises.name: Prone Y and T raise
exercises.cues: Thumbs up, lift with the lower and middle trapezius

exercises.name: Push-up plus progression (wall, incline, floor)
exercises.cues: Straight trunk, protract fully at the top

exercises.name: Single-leg squat and rotational medicine-ball work
exercises.cues: Control the knee and pelvis; transfer force through the trunk

exercises.name: Side plank
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30–45 s each side, 3 times per week
exercises.cues: Ribs down, hips level, shoulder blade set

progressionCriteria: External and internal rotation strength 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
Pain-free external rotation at 90° abduction under load
Good scapular control and single-leg control

stages.name: Plyometrics and interval throwing
goals: Return through a graded interval throwing program
Return to full training and competition
precautions: Increase distance, volume or intensity one at a time with a rest day between sessions
Stop and step back if posterior pain returns
After surgery, follow the surgeon's protocol; only 52% in one series returned to the previous level [r12]

exercises.name: Medicine-ball overhead throw and chest pass
Plyometric push-up or ball drops (reactive stability)
exercises.cues: Land with elbows slightly bent and shoulder blades set

exercises.name: Interval throwing program (distance, then volume, then intensity)
exercises.dosage: 3–4 sessions per week, graded over 6–12 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quality first; stop if posterior pain returns

exercises.name: Sport-specific drills with the full kinetic chain
exercises.dosage: Start at about 25–30% of normal volume and build over 4–6 weeks (clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Include the legs and trunk in the pattern

progressionCriteria: Completes the interval throwing program without pain
Strength, range and kinetic-chain tests meet return-to-sport criteria

criteria: Pain-free throwing through the full interval throwing program at match intensity
Total rotation arc symmetrical or within about 5° of the other shoulder, and no persistent symptomatic soft-tissue deficit (clinical convention)
External and internal rotation strength about 90% or more of the other side (clinical convention)
Kinetic-chain function: single-leg balance, trunk rotation and hip rotation
Agreed graded return of volume and intensity, with symptoms monitored over 24 hours
tests: Hand-held dynamometry for external rotation, internal rotation and scaption compared with the other side
Passive internal and external rotation and total arc at 90° abduction
Closed Kinetic Chain Upper Extremity Stability Test
Seated single-arm shot-put or medicine-ball throw
KJOC score at the end of rehabilitation [r12]

prognosis: Evidence is mostly observational and no controlled outcome data for non-operative care in symptomatic internal impingement were found. After arthroscopic surgery in 135 throwers (mean follow-up 7.9 years), 90% returned to sport but only 52% returned to the previous sport at the same level; male sex, an intra-operative cuff tear, no preoperative greater tuberosity cyst and cuff tear debridement were associated with a better return, and anterior capsulorrhaphy with worse postoperative pain [r12]. In an earlier series of 75 throwers treated with debridement, 60% were disappointed, only 12 resumed their former level with loaded arm movements, and 22 had another operation [r3]. Findings do not necessarily progress: none of the elite overhead athletes interviewed 5 years later had symptoms or needed treatment, although 8 of 20 dominant shoulders had MRI cuff tears at baseline [r5], and MRI findings in asymptomatic pitchers did not predict time on the disabled list [r6]. The long-term outcome of rehabilitation-treated symptomatic throwers was not quantified in the sources reviewed.
prevention: No trial of an injury-prevention program specifically for internal impingement was found; the following are clinical conventions
Monitor throwing workload and avoid sudden increases, with adequate rest between sessions
Maintain total rotation range and posterior shoulder mobility; a total rotation deficit of more than 5° was associated with more injury in professional pitchers [r15]
Maintain scapular, rotator cuff, trunk and lower-limb strength, since scapular dyskinesis contributes to internal impingement [r14]
Do not treat GIRD in isolation or in pain-free throwers without a deficit in the total arc [r8,r9]
clinicalPearls: Contact between the cuff undersurface and the posterosuperior glenoid is partly physiological, and cuff, labral and GIRD findings are common in pain-free throwers; do not treat the scan or the number [r3,r4,r5,r6].
GIRD is a measurement: measure the total arc, consider humeral retroversion, and note that GIRD alone is not clearly linked with injury [r8,r9,r7].
Stretching evidence is mainly in pain-free or non-athletic groups: cross-body stretch has moderate short-term evidence, the active sleeper stretch may be no better than no intervention [r10].
Scapular protraction with glenoid antetilt promotes posterior head translation and internal impingement, so assess and retrain the scapula and the kinetic chain, not only the posterior capsule [r14].
Surgery is not a reliable route back: only 52% returned to the previous sport at the same level after arthroscopy, and 60% were disappointed after debridement in an older series [r12,r3].
Consider coexisting SLAP, anterior microinstability and cuff lesions, and in adolescents consider Little League shoulder [r2].

animation.title: How internal impingement happens in a thrower

captions.text: A pitcher prepares to throw with the right arm.
In late cocking the arm is abducted and fully externally rotated.
The humeral head rotates back, and the cuff undersurface meets the back of the socket.
Acceleration follows, and thousands of repeated throws load the same contact point.
Some contact is normal; overload, tightness and poor scapular control can make it painful.
Zooming into the right shoulder, viewed from the front.

actions.label: Late cocking: cuff meets the glenoid rim

captions.text: The rotator cuff tendons lie against the top and back of the glenoid.
In late cocking the humeral head rotates back, so the cuff undersurface meets the socket rim.
Repeated overload can fray the posterosuperior labrum and the deep cuff.
Cysts or bone marrow change can appear on the humeral head.
A tight posterior capsule is proposed to shift the head back and add to the contact.
Many throwers show these changes without pain, so symptoms and function guide care.
Schematic of the cuff undersurface: healthy, aligned collagen.
Repeated overload causes a reactive response with swelling of the matrix.
With continued overload the matrix becomes disorganised: disrepair.
Areas of cell loss and disorganised matrix can form, often without symptoms.
With load management and training the tendon can regain capacity.
